articles.title: Automated, high-throughput kinematic analysis of skilled reaching in rodent models of neurological injury
articles.content: Neurological dysfunction can diminish quality of life by disrupting the movement capacity required to accomplish tasks. Kinematic studies guide treatment development by revealing subtle relationships between patterns of movement and neurological dysfunction. However, these studies produce a large quantity of opaque, multifaceted, and often highly correlated data. Here we present a novel and efficient approach to collecting, analyzing, and interpreting kinematic data with high throughput. We automated a single pellet reaching task in mice and created a video analysis pipeline that scores task success and extracts kinematic features from reaches. To analyze the resulting data, principal component analysis was first applied to group covarying measurements into a few overarching dimensions of behavior. Regularized regression was then applied separately to select reach qualities that best predicted task success. Applied to four nervous system injury models, this approach revealed differences in the effects of injury type and rehabilitative intervention on movement patterns that were not apparent from task success alone.
articles.author: Friedrich, L. S., Mendoza, E., Huie, J. R., Rosas, J., Wang, Z., Mathew, S., Schultz, C., Chhikara, N., Samburg, N., Specht, R., Antolak, I., Tsoulfas, P., Ferguson, A., Blackmore, M. G.

articles.title: MK-6240
articles.content: Flortaucipir and MK-6240 are two tau imaging agents currently in use for measuring neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) progression in Alzheimers disease (AD). The aims of this study were to use postmortem AD and Down syndrome (DS) brain sections to study three issues: (1) Measure binding affinity of flortaucipir and MK-6240 in AD brain sections by using [125I]IPPI; (2) Evaluate the binding characteristics of [18F]flortaucipir in AD, DS and cognitively normal (CN) brains sections and compare them with [18F]MK-6240, and (3) Assess the binding of [18F]flortaucipir in CN and Parkinsons disease (PD) brain sections to identify any off-target binding. The half-maximal inhibition (IC50) of [125I]IPPI bound to anterior cingulate (AC) in AD brain sections for flortaucipir was 2.91 nM and MK-6240 was 5.99 nM. Using frontal cortex (FCX) and temporal cortex (TCX) of AD, DS and CN brain sections, [18F]flortaucipir displayed high levels of binding in the gray matter (GM) of AD and DS. The average ratio of DSAD GM to CN GM was 15.7 in FCX, while DSAD GM to CN GM was 15.2 for the TCX. In the case of AD, average ratio of AD GM to CN GM was 12.4 in FCX, while AD GM to CN GM was 9.5 for the TCX. Binding of [18F]flortaucipir in brain section of AC from CN and PD cases did not exhibit any off-target binding to monoamine oxidase-A (MAO-A). In summary, both flortaucipir and MK-6240 exhibit similar high affinity to tau and [18F]flortaucipir exhibits higher binding compared to [18F]MK-6240 in DSAD.
articles.author: Biju, A. P., Herrera, J. M., McNamara, C. C., Hipolito, E. L. M., Liang, C., Mukherjee, J.

articles.title: Multisensory brain processing is associated with depressive symptoms in youth with chronic pain
articles.content: Juvenile fibromyalgia (JFM) is a chronic pain condition marked by widespread musculoskeletal pain and often accompanied by physical fatigue, nonrestorative sleep, headaches, anxiety, and depression. Previous studies have found that adolescents with fibromyalgia report augmented unpleasantness and altered brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimuli. Likewise, research in major depression has shown altered neural processing of sensory stimulation. We examined whether augmented brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimulation is associated with depressive symptoms in adolescent girls with JFM. Forty-six female adolescents with JFM (mean - SD, 16.43 - 1.10 years [range 13-18 years]) and 44 healthy participants (mean - SD, 16.09 - 1.06 years [range 13-18 years]) completed validated questionnaires assessing daily-life sensory hypersensitivity and depressive symptoms, alongside undergoing a functional MRI multisensory task. JFM patients reported significantly higher sensory unpleasantness than healthy participants, and this hypersensitivity was positively associated with depressive symptoms. Neuroimaging results in chronic pain patients revealed that greater depressive symptomatology was associated with increased activation in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) (pFWE<0.05), a region implicated in self-referential processing and specifically rumination in adults with chronic pain. JFM patients showed increased PCC-left middle temporal gyrus task-dependent connectivity using psychophysiological interactions analysis (PPI). Furthermore, hyperconnectivity between the PCC and brain areas involved in cognitive-affective regulation, sensory integration, and memory processing was strongly correlated with depressive symptoms in JFM patients. These findings underscore the role of depressive symptoms in sensory processing and integration in JFM patients and highlight the complex interplay between sensory processing and emotional/self-referential brain function in patients.
articles.author: Martin-Herrero, L., Sunol, M., Pascual-Diaz, S., Ting, T. V., Dudley, J. A., Jackson, C., Kashikar-Zuck, S., Coghill, R., Lopez Sola, M.

articles.title: Zona incerta drives a strategy of persistence during nocturnal predatory hunting in mice.
articles.content: Prey capture in lab mice is a complex, ethologically relevant behavior that provides us with an opportunity to study how mice integrate internal and external cues to drive goal-directed behaviors. Previous research has established that key parts of this behavior, such as the approach, are visually guided, but it has remained unknown how mice would perform if given exposure to hunting without visual cues. Zona incerta, a potential key locus for the integration of external and internal information, has previously been shown in naive mice to improve prey capture ability by increasing appetitive drive through integrating prey-related sensory information. It remains an open question if this region plays the same role in mice experienced with hunting in both the light and dark. Therefore, we examined the behavioral strategies used by mice with prior experience hunting in both the light and dark, as well as how these strategies are modulated by zona incerta. In experienced mice, we found that mice adjust their strategies to maintain similar success rates with and without visual cues, and that zona incerta further refines these strategies, specifically in the dark. This suggests that the role of zona incerta in these experienced mice is to maintain successful hunting by shifting behavioral strategies under ambiguous sensory conditions.
articles.author: Shallow, M. C., Wright, A. L., Weible, A. P., Smear, M. C., Wehr, M.

articles.title: Integrating multiple imputation with harmonization in multisite neuroimaging data: implications for site effects and biological inference
articles.content: Multisite neuroimaging harmonization in Alzheimer's disease research with missing data has received limited attention in the literature. Here, we evaluated the performance of several harmonization methods in conjunction with multiple imputation (MI) to address missing data, using baseline [18F]flortaucipir tau positron emission tomography (PET) data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We compared complete case and MICE-imputed datasets (m = 5) across the original ADNI-preprocessed data and four statistical harmonization approaches: ComBat with and without covariates, quantile normalization, and quantile regression. Weighted average standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) across six Braak regions were analyzed for each dataset-method combination. We assessed harmonization effectiveness using covariate-adjusted intraclass correlation coefficients and site-level pairwise differences, and evaluated biological effect preservation using Hedges' g, regression coefficients, and statistical significance for comparisons between cognitively impaired and unimpaired participants. For imputed analyses, effect sizes and regression coefficients were pooled using Rubin's rules, with statistical inference based on the pooled estimates. Post-processing harmonization reduced site-level variability compared to the original data, with method performance varying across evaluation metrics, while overall harmonization quality remained comparable after MI. Disease group differences remained statistically significant across all combinations, exhibiting a consistent regional pattern, strongest in Braak I and weakest in Braak VI. MI modestly increased effect size and coefficient estimates, with improved precision reflected by median standard error ratios below 1 (0.89 for effect sizes and 0.93 for coefficients). These findings indicate that integrating MI with harmonization preserves disease group differences and improves statistical efficiency without compromising harmonization performance, supporting a practical framework for multisite neuroimaging studies.
articles.author: Ren, Y., Dong, Y., Minhas, D., Cohen, A. D., Wu, Q., Tudorascu, D. L.

articles.title: Adaptation can explain cortical responses to sound deviance without requiring prediction
articles.content: Sensory systems amplify what is rare, allowing animals to orient toward threats and opportunities hidden among regular events. Whether this deviance detection reflects neuronal adaptation or error against the brain's predictive model is debated. The two processes can contribute simultaneously because the context that enables prediction also drives adaptation. To dissociate them, we recorded from primary auditory cortex neurons in awake mice during a modified oddball paradigm that separated recent sound history from longer-term sequence statistics. Contextual effects ranged from suppression to facilitation of responses. Facilitation increased with deviance magnitude, as expected for prediction error. However, neither facilitation, suppression, nor stimulus-specific adaptation depended on these longer-term statistics. A normalization model in which a neuron's inputs adapt at different rates reproduced the range of contextual effects and their weakening in background noise. Adaptive normalization can therefore generate deviance signals, including facilitation, without requiring a predictive model.
articles.author: Jarzebowski, P., Bishnoi, A., Bendor, D.

articles.title: Whole-mount three-dimensional imaging and quantitative analysis platform for early brain development using dorsal forebrain spheroids
articles.content: Three-dimensional culture systems have emerged as a bridge between in vitro and in vivo models. Organoids and spheroids derived from human stem cells can model cellular interactions, morphology and organization of the neocortex, and provide a platform for future translational research into neurological disorders. However, the heterogeneity commonly found in 3D culture systems presents considerable challenges for identifying significant, reproducible, and disorder-relevant phenotypes. Here, we present a rigorous methodological framework for the longitudinal analysis of dorsal forebrain spheroids, beginning with gross spheroid morphology, extending to structural phenotypes in rosette morphogenesis, and culminating in cellular analyses of neural progenitor cell proliferation and cell cycle dynamics. This workflow integrates isogenic iPSC-derived spheroid culture, whole-mount optical clearing, high-resolution 3D imaging and reconstruction, and cumulative EdU-labeling assays. Testing the sensitivity of this approach in an isogenic Down syndrome model, we reliably detected new features of altered spheroid growth, delayed rosette emergence, reduced rosette density, and prolonged progenitor cell cycle progression. This approach provides a reproducible strategy for measuring complex developmental phenotypes in 3D culture models and can be applied to neurodevelopmentally altered cell lines beyond Down syndrome.
articles.author: Ayoub, A., Lu, L. X., Haydar, T. F.

articles.title: Whole-bulb LSFEM enables automated reconstruction and quantitative spatial mapping of thousands of olfactory glomeruli
articles.content: The glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb (OB) transforms chemical information into the first spatially organized neural representation of odor identity. Yet its three-dimensional architecture remains difficult to quantify at whole-bulb scale. Here, we establish an end-to-end framework integrating light-sheet fluorescence expansion microscopy (LSFEM) with automated reconstruction of thousands of individual glomeruli across intact mouse OBs. LSFEM preserves whole-bulb architecture and supports genetically encoded fluorescence and immunolabelling, providing continuous multichannel input for automated analysis. SegFormer-based segmentation of 2D optical sections was followed by morphology-guided separation and three-dimensional object reconstruction. Across 12 intact bulbs, the workflow yielded a median of 2,677 glomeruli per bulb, approaching the 2,851 reported by complete three-dimensional reconstruction. Object-level maps further revealed that glomeruli spanning a broad range of volumes were intermingled throughout the bulb without evident size-defined anatomical domains. Because each reconstructed glomerulus retains a three-dimensional centroid coordinate, the resulting object map can additionally be used as a specimen-specific spatial reference framework, allowing distances and distributions to be expressed relative to defined glomerular or anatomical positions within the intact OB. Together, whole-bulb LSFEM and automated reconstruction provide a scalable framework for quantitative three-dimensional mapping of glomerular number, morphology, and spatial organization, and the relative positioning of additional anatomical signals within the glomerular architecture.
articles.author: Rodriguez-Gatica, J. E., Jayakumar, J. I., Gnanasekar, S. I., Mohammadi, A., Ackels, T., Rothermel, M., Roos, D., Schwarz, M. K.

articles.title: Partial microglial depletion attenuates Purkinje cell degeneration and reshapes both glial and inflammatory responses in a mouse model of selective neurodegeneration
articles.content: Background The microglial population contributes to the inflammatory environment during neurodegeneration. Its role in neuronal loss remains hard to distinguish from its response to injury. We investigated how early pharmacological reduction of this population affects Purkinje cell preservation, behaviour and the cerebellar glial response. Methods We administered PLX5622 to Purkinje cell degeneration (PCD) and wild-type (WT) mice from postnatal day (P) 15 to P24 and compared them with their respective untreated controls. We assessed motor coordination, spontaneous behaviours and novel-object recognition at P17, P21 and P25. At P25, we quantified regional Purkinje cell preservation, glial immunoreactivity and microglial abundance and morphology. We assessed selected transcripts in whole-cerebellum samples by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Results At P25, treated PCD mice showed better motor coordination, improvements in selected spontaneous behaviours and greater novel-object discrimination. Greater Purkinje cell preservation coincided with lower glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) immunoreactivity in lobes IV-V and VIII. Microglial density decreased in all four PCD regions analysed. The territory encompassed by the processes of residual microglia expanded in both genotypes. In PCD mice, CD68-positive tissue area decreased in lobes I-II and IV-V, and the proportion of Iba1-positive area occupied by CD68 decreased in IV-V. CD45, CD16/32 and CD206 immunoreactivity decreased alongside selective reductions in immune, inflammatory and phagocytosis-associated transcripts. Treated WT mice showed early behavioural changes, including reduced novel-object discrimination. Conclusions Early PLX5622 treatment can modify the outcome of genetically driven cerebellar degeneration in PCD mice. The benefits achieved with partial microglial depletion provide a preclinical rationale for testing how the timing and extent of glial modulation influence neuronal protection during active degeneration.
articles.author: Perez-Boyero, D., Perez-Arevalo, J., Valero, J., Weruaga, E., Diaz, D.

articles.title: Social Connection: Resting-State Functional Connectivity Associations with Social Networks, and the Roles of Empathy and Sex
articles.content: Smaller social networks (SNs) negatively influence cognition, psychiatric trajectories and mortality. Studies linking SNs to resting-state functional connectivity (FC) inconsistently suggest orbito-frontal and frontoparietal regions and implicate a potential role for empathy and sex. We investigate how SN characteristics relate to FC, additionally assessing if empathy and sex alter these associations. Group-independent component analysis was applied to multi-band resting-state fMRI from 83 participants (Caltech Conte dataset: ds003798). The Social Network Index measures SN-contacts (SN-contacts) SN-diversity (number of roles) and SN-embeddedness (number of contact groups) and the Empathy Quotient measured empathy. Using MANCOVA, we investigate if resting-state network power and connectivity are associated with SNI measures and whether these relationships differ by empathizing ability and sex. Participants aged 18-48 (mean age 29.3+/-7.0, 55% male) demonstrated SN-contacts and SN-diversity associated with lower frontal-pole FC within the default-mode network (DMN, q-values<0.05). Empathy altered how SN-diversity and SN-contacts relate to superior lateral-occipital, default mode and salience network FC (q-values<0.05). Finally, males and females showed diverging associations of SN-contacts and SN-diversity with salience network power. Smaller SNs were associated with increased anterior-DMN FC, potentially indicating a tendency towards internally-directed cognition in more socially isolated individuals. Opposing relationships between SNs with salience and lateral-frontoparietal networks by empathy level highlights empathy as critical for understanding social biology. Males and females differed in SN associations with salience network coherency, supporting known sex-specific neural correlates of social behavior. These findings provide insights into the biology of social networks, offering potential targets for studying social deficits in psychiatric populations.
